title: Low-Grade Inflammation as a Transdiagnostic Pathway in Neurological and Psychiatric Disorders: The Role of Environmental Risk Factors and Biomarker-Based
content: Low-grade inflammation refers to the chronic activation of the immune system, characterized by persistently elevated levels of pro-inflammatory mediators, in contrast to the pronounced inflammatory response observed during acute infections, which typically resolves and returns to baseline. Low-grade inflammation is often subclinical and remains undiagnosed, yet it may affect psychiatric and neurological outcomes. Low-grade inflammation has been observed in a range of disorders, including cardiovascular disease, cancer, metabolic and autoimmune diseases such as diabetes and multiple sclerosis (MS), as well as psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders, including mood disorders, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder. Environmental risk factors contributing to low-grade inflammation include viral infections, vitamin D deficiency, obesity, smoking, gut microbiome dysbiosis, dietary imbalances, and psychosocial stress. Identifying low-grade inflammation may help reduce the disease burden by addressing underlying contributing factors, including infections, vitamin D deficiency, inadequate nutrition, smoking, and chronic stress. Depending on the underlying condition, disease-specific management may involve anti-inflammatory therapies, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, disease-modifying immunomodulatory agents, metabolic interventions, and adjunctive nutritional or dietary supplementation. However, actionable biomarkers for guiding treatment decisions in psychiatry remain limited. Commonly used biomarkers of inflammation include C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), white blood cell count, platelet count, and fibrinogen. An innovative combinatorial biomarker signature of inflammation comprises low levels of vitamin D, elevated levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) and interleukin-8 (IL-8), which was initially described in patients with MS and subsequently detected in patients with schizophrenia. These findings highlight the potential of transdiagnostic approaches for identifying shared underlying disease mechanisms, including low-grade inflammation. Future research should focus on identifying and validating biomarker signatures for low-grade inflammation that enable patient stratification and help optimize personalized treatment strategies.
